Where is Eagle Mountain, Utah?

Eagle Mountain is a city in northwest Utah County, in the flat Cedar Valley west and north of the Lake Mountains, and it belongs to the Provo-Orem metropolitan area. It covers about 50 square miles at an elevation of roughly 4,885 feet.

Because the city is in Utah County, your tax bill, deed recording and property records all run through Provo, the county seat. The Utah County treasurer and recorder both work from the county building at 100 East Center Street in Provo.

How did Eagle Mountain become a city so quickly?

In 1994 three investors bought about 8,000 acres at a bankruptcy auction in western Utah County, and on December 3, 1996 the area incorporated as the Town of Eagle Mountain. It was renamed Eagle Mountain City in 2001, and in 2011 it annexed the White Hills neighborhood and nearly 2,900 acres.

The census numbers show how fast it moved.

  • 2000: 2,157 residents
  • 2010: 21,415 residents
  • 2020: 43,623 residents
  • July 1, 2025: an estimated 66,557 residents (Census Bureau)

The city still holds traces of older history, including a site on the original Pony Express trail and a boulder with petroglyphs carved by the Fremont people about 1,800 years ago.

What drives the Eagle Mountain economy?

Data centers are the most visible employer. Meta broke ground on its Eagle Mountain campus in 2018, began operations in 2021 and, in September 2026, confirmed a further expansion that brings its Utah investment above $3 billion. The company says construction will peak at about 1,200 jobs and that more than 300 permanent roles will follow, though those are company figures.

QTS and Google also have data center operations or plans here, and the developer Tract bought 668 acres in 2024 for future campuses. A 150-megawatt battery storage project is expected online later in 2026.

Meta also projects that it will become one of Eagle Mountain's largest property taxpayers. For a house seller, the useful takeaway is that a large employer is still adding jobs nearby, which keeps newcomers looking for homes.

The 2020 census found a median age of 22.4 and 44.7% of residents under 18. With 4.18 people in the average household and 84.7% of homes owner-occupied, most houses here are lived in by their owners rather than rented out.

Which school district serves Eagle Mountain?

Today the Alpine School District serves Eagle Mountain, but that changes on July 1, 2027, when the district splits into three. Eagle Mountain, Saratoga Springs, Cedar Fort and Fairfield will form the Lake Mountain School District, while Lehi, American Fork, Highland, Alpine and Cedar Hills go to Aspen Peaks and Orem, Pleasant Grove, Lindon and Vineyard go to Timpanogos.

Current schools include eight elementary schools, Frontier Middle School and Cedar Valley High School, which opened in August 2019, along with charter schools such as The Ranches Academy, John Hancock Charter School and Rockwell Charter High School. If you are selling during the transition, expect buyers to ask which district the address will land in, and send them to the district office for current boundary maps.

How do roads and climate shape life in Eagle Mountain?

The main routes are SR-73, Pony Express Parkway, Eagle Mountain Boulevard and Ranches Parkway. The Mountain View Corridor segment linking the Salt Lake and Utah valleys was completed in December 2025, and UTA has run express bus Route 806 since 2008.

Rainfall is light. The Ranches area averages about 16.75 inches of precipitation a year, and the city center is drier, cooler and has colder nights, with a combined average July high of 90 degrees. Buyers usually ask for the roof's age, so have that date handy.

What are Eagle Mountain's rules for accessory units and short-term rentals?

Eagle Mountain allows accessory dwelling units, but not in townhomes, duplexes or apartments, and an ADU permit is required in addition to any building permit.

  • The unit needs its own kitchen, bathroom and separate entrance.
  • The owner must live in either the main home or the ADU, with temporary absences allowed.
  • The site plan must show two off-street parking spaces.
  • The application fee is $230.
  • ADUs cannot be rented for fewer than 30 consecutive days.

Unpermitted units are treated as illegal until an application is approved. Short-term rentals of any kind also carry a 1% transient room tax under city code, with records kept for at least three years. Unpaid amounts add a 10% penalty and 12% annual interest, and the operator's business license can be revoked.

How are property taxes and deed recording handled in Eagle Mountain?

Utah County sets the dates: the Auditor mails valuation notices around July 22, Board of Equalization appeals are due September 1, tax notices go out in the third week of October, and real property taxes are due November 30. Mailed payments count if they carry a U.S. Post Office postmark, but a postage meter mark from an office does not.

On December 1, delinquent parcels are charged the greater of $10 or 1%. Utah residents also get the state's 45% primary residential exemption, so tax is based on 55% of a primary home's value.

Deeds are recorded with the Utah County Recorder in Provo, which charges a $40 standard fee per document plus $2 for each description over ten. Credit and debit cards carry a 2.65% processing fee, while electronic checks do not.

What should an Eagle Mountain seller gather before talking to a buyer?

A short folder of papers saves days later. Start with the parcel number from your Utah County tax notice, since every county lookup depends on it.

  • The most recent tax notice and proof of payment.
  • The ADU permit or the application receipt, if the house has a second unit.
  • Transient room tax records, if you ever rented the house for stays under 30 days.
  • Any HOA contact, loan payoff details and the roof's age.

Eagle Mountain also has four regional parks and about 35 local parks, and the Mountain Ranch Bike Park opened in 2009 as the first of its kind on the Wasatch Front. Neighborhood amenities like these are worth a line in any listing or offer discussion.

How does a cash sale work in Eagle Mountain?

A cash sale means no mortgage underwriting, so closing depends on title work alone.

  1. Send the address and a few details about the house.
  2. We review the property and nearby sales.
  3. You accept or decline the offer.
  4. A title company prepares the paperwork and sets a closing date.
  5. The deed is recorded in Provo and you are paid at closing.

A house with an unpermitted ADU or an unfinished basement can be hard for a financed buyer to close on. With no lender involved, the condition of the house is between you and us.

More questions about Eagle Mountain, UT

What county is Eagle Mountain in?

Utah County. Eagle Mountain is in northwest Utah County, so property taxes and recording go through the county offices in Provo.

When are property taxes due in Eagle Mountain?

November 30. Utah County lists that date as the due date for real property taxes, and delinquent parcels are penalized beginning December 1.

Which school district will Eagle Mountain be in after 2027?

The Lake Mountain School District. It takes over from Alpine School District on July 1, 2027 and also covers Saratoga Springs, Cedar Fort and Fairfield.

Can I rent my Eagle Mountain basement apartment short term?

No, not as an ADU. Eagle Mountain requires ADU rentals to run at least 30 consecutive days, and other short-term rentals owe a 1% transient room tax.

What does it cost to record a deed in Utah County?

The standard fee is $40 per document, with $2 for each additional description over ten. The Recorder will not record a document until the fees are paid or authorized electronically.

Where is Herriman, Utah?

Herriman is a city in the southwest corner of Salt Lake County, bordered by Riverton to the east, South Jordan to the north and Bluffdale to the southeast. It covers about 23 square miles at roughly 5,000 feet of elevation.

The city has no post office of its own. Mail goes through the Riverton Post Office at 12760 S 2080 W, so check that closing documents use the right address. City Hall is at 5355 West Herriman Main Street, and the offices are open 7:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. on weekdays.

How fast did Herriman grow, and what does that mean for sellers?

Herriman grew from 1,523 residents in 2000 to 21,785 in 2010 and 55,144 in 2020, and the Census Bureau estimates 63,282 as of July 1, 2025. That jump moved the city from the 111th-largest incorporated place in Utah to the 14th-largest in two decades.

Most of the housing here is therefore recent. A development company, Rosecrest, drove much of the early building, and in 2007 a lawsuit let the city annex about 4,000 acres from Bluffdale. The city kept annexing, most recently the 933-acre Olympia development in 2022.

For a seller, newer construction usually means fewer old-house surprises. A house that needs work, or has a tenant or a title problem, is the kind of listing a financed buyer tends to pass over.

Residents petitioned for incorporation in 1999, and Herriman became a city on April 19, 2001.

  • The application review fee is $559, plus a building permit fee that depends on the area remodeled.
  • Plan review takes about 7 to 14 business days.
  • The owner signs a notarized affidavit that is recorded with the County Recorder.

November 30. Salt Lake County lists that as the last day to pay without penalty, and unpaid taxes are delinquent from December 1.

Where is Draper, Utah, and why does the county line matter when you sell?

Draper sits on the Wasatch Front about 20 miles south of Salt Lake City, and the city spans two counties: Salt Lake County and Utah County. It covers roughly 30 square miles at an elevation of 4,751 feet, with Sandy to the north, South Jordan to the northwest, Riverton and Bluffdale to the west, and Lehi, Highland and Alpine to the south and southeast.

The city describes itself as sitting at the Point of the Mountain, the narrow gap between the south end of the Salt Lake Valley and the north end of Utah Valley. For a seller, the county line decides which assessor values the house, which treasurer sends the tax bill and which recorder files the deed. The school district changes too: the Salt Lake County side is served by Canyons School District and the Utah County side by Alpine School District.

Check your parcel number before you plan anything. Two neighbors a few blocks apart can deal with different county offices, different tax calendars and different school boundaries.

What is the history of Draper in brief?

Draper began as a cattle and farming settlement in the fall of 1849, when Ebenezer Brown grazed cattle near South Willow Creek. His wife's brother, William Draper Jr., joined the family in 1850, and about twenty families lived in the area by the end of 1852.

The first post office opened in 1854 under the name Draperville. That same year Ebenezer Brown gave land near 12650 South 900 East for a fort, though the walls were never finished. By the 1940s the town was known as the Egg Basket of Utah, and Draper became a city in 1978.

The growth since then is striking. The 2020 census counted 51,017 people in Draper, up from 7,257 in 1990. Many of the neighborhoods you see today were built in that window, so houses in the city range from old farm lots to subdivisions less than a generation old.

What does the Draper economy look like?

Draper is part of the Silicon Slopes tech corridor, and the city reports more than 1,000 businesses. Company headquarters or major offices named in public sources include 1-800 Contacts, Control4, HealthEquity, Pluralsight and Synchrony Bank, along with Dealertrack, Trader Joe's and Tesla in the city's own list. Utah's first IKEA opened in Draper in 2007.

The Utah State Prison operated in Draper from 1951 to 2022, and it ranked in the top employer size band (1,000 to 1,999 workers) in a fiscal 2018 snapshot.

Getting around is straightforward by Utah standards. Interstate 15 runs through the area, UTA's TRAX Blue Line stops at Draper Town Center and Kimballs Lane, and a FrontRunner commuter rail station is also in the city. Salt Lake International Airport and Provo Municipal Airport are each about 30 minutes away by car, according to the city.

Does wildfire risk affect a Draper house sale?

It can, especially for homes along the foothills. In December 2025 the Draper City Council adopted Ordinance 1695, which created a Wildland Urban Interface Area in the city code. The public notice does not map the boundaries or list the rules, so ask the city for the full ordinance if your lot backs onto open hillside.

A separate state program adds another layer. Utah House Bill 48 of 2025 led the state forestry division to publish a wildfire risk map that scores each building from 1 to 8. A building that scores 7 or higher and sits within 250 meters of at least two other buildings falls inside the high-risk boundary, and owners of those buildings may owe the state an annual fee once the program starts, which the state expected later in 2026.

  • Look up the address at wildfirerisk.utah.gov before you list or accept an offer.
  • Keep a printout of the score for the buyer or title company.

What are Draper's rules for short-term rentals and accessory units?

Draper requires two approvals to run a short-term rental: a business license and a short-term rental permit. A stay counts as short term when it is under 30 consecutive days, the minimum stay is two nights, and the permit has to be renewed every year. Each day of unpermitted operation is a separate violation.

Accessory dwelling units have their own limits.

  • A detached ADU needs a residential lot of at least 12,000 square feet.
  • An internal ADU generally needs a residential lot over 6,000 square feet on a qualifying street, and the city has mapped areas where internal units are banned.
  • The owner must live in the main dwelling for both types.
  • Rentals of an ADU must run at least 30 consecutive days, and each needs one extra on-site parking space.

A basement apartment that was built without a permit is a common snag. The city's ADU page says owners who did not apply by February 1, 2022 face immediate enforcement, so a buyer who needs financing may hesitate over one. Draper's planning office takes questions at (801) 576-6399.

How are property taxes handled on a Draper home?

Your county's calendar controls the bill, and Utah gives primary residences a 45% exemption so that only 55% of market value is taxed. Rental homes can qualify as primary residences under the state's rules, while vacation homes cannot.

For a Salt Lake County parcel, the county lists these dates:

  • July 22: valuation notices are mailed.
  • August 1 to September 15: the Board of Equalization takes valuation appeals.
  • November 1: official tax notices go out.
  • November 30: last day to pay without penalty.
  • December 1: unpaid taxes become delinquent, with a penalty of the greater of 2.5% or $10 per parcel.

A Utah County parcel follows the same November 30 due date, with notices mailed around the third week of October. Delinquent parcels in Utah County face a penalty of $10 or 1%, whichever is greater, on December 1. If your house is on the market when the notice arrives, tell the title officer so the current-year bill is handled correctly at closing.

How does a cash sale work in Draper?

A cash sale in Draper follows the same steps as any Utah sale, minus the lender. You give us the address and a few details, we review the house, and if the offer works you pick the closing date with a title company.

  1. Tell us about the house, including any tenants, liens or repairs.
  2. We look at the property and the recent sales around it.
  3. You decide whether to accept the offer or walk away.
  4. A title company runs the title search and prepares the closing paperwork.
  5. The deed is recorded with the county recorder where the parcel sits.

Recording is cheap. Salt Lake County charges a flat $40 recording fee, and Utah County lists the same $40 standard fee per document. Salt Lake County asks for a notary acknowledgment, the grantee's address and the tax serial number on the deed.

What do Draper sellers usually run into?

A short list of issues tends to slow a Draper sale.

  • A hillside lot with a high state wildfire score.
  • An older basement unit with no ADU permit.
  • A short-term rental permit that lapsed after its annual renewal.
  • A tenant in place on a rental, since roughly 31% of occupied homes are not owner-occupied.
  • Confusion over whether the parcel is billed by Salt Lake County or Utah County.

Any of these can be solved, but each adds steps to a traditional listing. A direct sale lets you sell the house as it stands and deal with the paperwork at the title company.

Both. Draper lies in Salt Lake County and Utah County, so the county for your tax bill and deed depends on the parcel. Look up the parcel number on your tax notice to see which county applies.

When are Draper property taxes due?

November 30, whichever county bills you. Salt Lake County lists November 30 as the last day to pay without penalty, and Utah County does the same. If the date falls on a weekend or holiday it moves to the next business day.

Do I need a permit to rent my Draper house on a short-term basis?

Yes. Draper requires both a business license and a short-term rental permit, and the permit must be renewed each year. Operating without both is a violation, and each day counts separately.

Can I sell a Draper house that has an unpermitted basement apartment?

Yes, you can sell it, but expect questions. Draper requires an ADU permit before an accessory unit is rented, and the owner must live in the main dwelling. A cash buyer can take the house as it is, while a bank-financed buyer may ask you to resolve the permit first.

How do I check wildfire risk for a Draper address?

Search the address at wildfirerisk.utah.gov. The portal shows a structure exposure score from 1 to 8, and the state treats buildings scoring 7 or higher near other buildings as high risk.

Where is Bountiful, Utah, and how is the city laid out?

Bountiful is a city in Davis County, Utah, built on the slope between the Wasatch Range and the Great Salt Lake flats. Its elevation is about 4,771 feet, and the city covers roughly 13 square miles.

The original downtown sits at the base of the mountains. Homes climb the benches to the east, and the land to the west is flat and runs out toward the lake. Most of the ground east of the city is U.S. Forest Service land, so the hillside streets end where public land begins.

North Salt Lake lies to the south, Woods Cross and West Bountiful to the west, and Centerville to the north. Val Verda is the name used for the area in the southern part of the city. A seller on a bench street and a seller on the west side are dealing with very different lots, and buyers know it.

How did Bountiful start, and how fast has it grown?

Perrigrine Sessions and his family settled the site on September 27, 1847, which made it the second settlement in Utah after Salt Lake City. The place was first called Sessions Settlement and North Canyon Ward, and it was renamed Bountiful in 1855. The city incorporated in 1892, and electric lights came in 1907.

Growth was slow for a long time and then fast. The census counted 6,004 residents in 1950 and 17,039 in 1960. Bountiful was the largest city in Davis County until 1985, when Layton passed it.

Bountiful has a dry climate with about 23 inches of precipitation and about 59 inches of snow in a typical year. The record high is 104 degrees and the record low is minus 9, so roofs, furnaces and cooling systems all get used.

Heavy snow matters most on older roofs and on shaded driveways. Buyers and inspectors in a snow climate often look at the roof surface, the attic insulation and the gutters first. A seller who has not touched those in years should expect questions.

The Wasatch Fault runs along the base of the range, and the Utah Division of Emergency Management says more than 85 percent of Utahns live in the earthquake zone along the Wasatch Front. Interstate 15 is the main road, and the FrontRunner commuter rail has served Bountiful since April 2008. The Legacy Parkway opened on September 13, 2008, to take pressure off I-15. Other local anchors include Lakeview Hospital, the Bountiful Utah Temple (dedicated in 1995) and Mueller Park Canyon with its popular trail. Houses within a short drive of the canyon trailheads tend to get extra attention from buyers who hike.

You file a Board of Equalization appeal with the Davis County Controller by the deadline printed on your Notice of Property Market Valuation. The county's online form takes one application per parcel, and it asks you to state your own opinion of the value as of January 1.

The county lists the kinds of evidence it accepts. A recent closing statement, a full appraisal, at least three comparable sales within one mile, an income statement, a documented factual error or a record of a damaged condition can each support a case. Only the current year's market value can be appealed, not the tax rate. The controller's phone number is 801-451-3323.

If you sell mid-year, the appeal and the tax bill still follow the property. Tell the buyer's side what is pending so the title company can handle any refund correctly.

Bountiful's resale pool is large because the city is close to Salt Lake City and has the FrontRunner line. That helps a well-kept house on the market. It does less for a property that needs work, which is where an as-is sale tends to fit.

Where is Cedar City, Utah, and what is it like to live there?

Cedar City is the largest city in Iron County, in southwestern Utah, about 250 miles south of Salt Lake City and 170 miles north of Las Vegas on Interstate 15. It sits in Cedar Valley on the western edge of the Markagunt Plateau, at an elevation above 5,600 feet.

St. George is about 50 miles to the southwest, and Interstate 70 is about 75 miles north. Zion National Park, Bryce Canyon National Park and Cedar Breaks National Monument are all within a day trip. The name comes from the juniper trees early settlers called cedars.

Most buyers here either work in town, attend the university, or are drawn by the access to the parks and the high country. A seller who knows which group their house suits can talk about it more plainly.

How did Cedar City begin, and how big is it now?

Cedar City was founded on November 11, 1851, when Mormon pioneers from Parowan came to build an iron works. The town moved to a new site closer to the works in 1855, out of the Coal Creek flood plain. It incorporated on February 18, 1868, and a railroad connection in 1923 made it a gateway for park visitors. Mining continued until the 1980s.

A young median age reflects the university. It also means plenty of rentals, which matters if you are a landlord thinking about selling.

What does the economy depend on in Cedar City?

Cedar City's economy rests on Southern Utah University, a small manufacturing base, tourism and home construction. SUU is the largest employer in Iron County, and the Iron County School District is next in the 2019 employer list.

  • Southern Utah University: 2,000 to 2,999 employees
  • Iron County School District: 1,000 to 1,999
  • Intermountain Health: 500 to 1,500
  • Cedar City Corporation, Genpak, federal government, State of Utah and Walmart: 250 to 499 each

SUU reported a fall 2025 headcount of 15,825 students, up 2.47 percent from the year before, including more than 3,691 fully online students. A Gardner Policy Institute study of fiscal year 2023 counted 2,687 direct SUU jobs and more than 5,000 jobs once indirect effects were included. The same study put out-of-region visitor spending at about $7 million, tied to events such as the Utah Shakespeare Festival and athletics.

Because a lot of the local economy follows the school calendar and the festival season, demand for houses and rentals can shift with the term and the summer. That is worth knowing before you set a closing date.

What does Cedar City's weather mean for a house?

Cedar City has a semi-arid climate with cold winters, hot summers and about 11 inches of precipitation a year. In the 1991 to 2020 normals, the January daily high averages 42.8 degrees and the low 18.0, while July highs average 91.0.

Snow is a real factor. The city averages about 47.8 inches a year, and January 1949 holds the single-month record of 36.9 inches. The record low is minus 26 and the record high is 105.

That range is hard on exteriors. Freeze and thaw cycles crack driveways and stucco, dry summers fade roofing, and cold nights stress older plumbing and water heaters. Buyers who tour in winter will notice insulation, windows and heating costs quickly.

  • Roof condition after heavy snow seasons
  • Exposed pipes and hose bibs in cold snaps
  • Cracks in concrete and stucco from freeze and thaw
  • Heating system age and efficiency

Which schools, roads and services does Cedar City have?

The Iron County School District serves Cedar City, with two high schools, Cedar High School and Canyon View High School. Southern Utah University is the main college, and the city is also known for the Utah Shakespeare Festival and the Utah Summer Games.

Interstate 15 is the main route. A Union Pacific branch line runs along the western edge of town, and the Cedar City Regional Airport has Delta Connection flights. The city also has a local bus system. Cedar City Utah Temple was dedicated on December 10, 2017.

City Hall is at 10 North Main Street, open 8 am to 5 pm. The City Council meets on Wednesdays at 5:30 pm and streams on YouTube, except on the fifth Wednesday of a month. The city runs a water usage app called MY360 that lets residents view their water use, which is handy when closing out an account.

Iron County assesses and bills Cedar City homes, and its offices are at 68 South 100 East in Parowan. The Assessor is at 435-477-8310. The county says property is valued by its condition and ownership as of January 1, using cost, income and market approaches.

Appeals go through the Iron County Auditor at 435-477-8333. Unpaid current-year taxes become delinquent on December 1, and Utah's property tax calendar describes a tax sale for parcels that stay unpaid for years. A seller with back taxes should talk to the treasurer before listing.

What else is in Iron County besides Cedar City?

Iron County covers about 3,300 square miles along Utah's western border with Nevada, and Parowan is the county seat. The 2020 census counted 57,289 people in the county, so Cedar City holds most of them. Enoch and Parowan are the other named towns nearby.

The county runs from desert basins in the west to high plateau meadows and forest in the east. Brian Head, at 11,307 feet, is the highest point and Cedar Breaks National Monument sits on the Markagunt Plateau. A seller on the east side of town and a seller near the desert edge can face very different weather, so say which one you are when you describe the house.

What do Cedar City sellers usually face?

Cedar City sellers often have a rental that has aged, a house that needs updating, or a property they inherited from a family member who lived out of state. Selling for cash can fit those cases because there is no lender appraisal and no list of buyer repair requests.

  • Houses with older roofs, windows and heating systems

If the house is vacant, winter matters. A cold, empty house can freeze pipes, and a summer-vacant one can pick up dust and weeds quickly. Many sellers in a spot like this want one clear closing date instead of months of showings.

Cedar City is in Iron County, and the Iron County Assessor sets the value. The assessor's office is in Parowan at 68 South 100 East, and the phone number is 435-477-8310.

Iron County real property appeals are due September 15 by 5:00 PM, or 45 days after the valuation notice is mailed if that is later. File with the Iron County Auditor at 435-477-8333.

Property tax is due November 30, and unpaid taxes become delinquent on December 1. Iron County mails the tax notices around November 1.

Cedar City had 35,235 residents at the 2020 census, and the Census Bureau estimated 41,871 for July 1, 2025. It is the largest city in Iron County.

Yes, a house can be sold with tenants in place or after they leave. Share the lease dates and rent details early so the closing date and move-out terms are agreed in writing.

Where is Kearns, Utah?

Kearns is a city on the west side of the Salt Lake Valley, bordered by West Valley City to the north and west, Taylorsville to the east and West Jordan to the south. It covers 4.63 square miles, all land, at an elevation of about 4,530 feet.

How did an Army base become Kearns?

Kearns began on May 1, 1942, as Kearns Army Air Base, a World War II training facility for the U.S. Army Air Forces named for Utah Senator Thomas Kearns. The land before then was dry farmland that had been set aside for universities and colleges.

The base was renamed Camp Kearns on January 1, 1944, and it was deactivated on August 15, 1946, when the Air Force transferred it to the State of Utah. Developers then built homes and businesses on the former base land, and Kearns grew into what Wikipedia calls the first suburb in Salt Lake County.

Earthquakes are the other concern. The Wasatch fault is Utah's most active, and the Utah Geological Survey says liquefaction is most likely in low-lying central parts of a valley, especially near lakes and stream corridors where groundwater is shallow. Susceptible soils are loose, young, sandy or silty deposits that are saturated within about 30 to 50 feet of the surface. Where is Clearfield, Utah, and what does the map look like?

Clearfield is a compact city in north-central Davis County, about 30 miles north of Salt Lake City, with Hill Air Force Base along its northeastern edge. It covers roughly 7.75 square miles, which makes it one of the smaller cities on the north Wasatch Front.

The Weber and Davis Canal runs along the east and northeast edge. Interstate 15 follows the eastern side of town, and the Wasatch Range rises beyond it, with Ben Lomond Peak at 9,712 feet.

Richard and Emily Hamblin settled the area in 1877 and called it Sand Ridge. The Utah Central Railroad crossed the area in 1869, and a canal that arrived in 1884 sparked a population jump. Clearfield became a town on July 17, 1922, and a city on March 21, 1946.

War changed the place. Hill Field began construction in 1940, and the Navy commissioned the Clearfield Naval Supply Depot on April 10, 1943, to supply the Pacific Fleet. The Navy phased the depot out in 1962, and private firms moved in. That site is now the Freeport Center.

Because the city is small and flat, many houses are a short drive from the base gates, the Freeport Center and the freeway. That convenience is one of the first things buyers ask about.

Hill Air Force Base borders Clearfield, Layton, Riverdale, Roy and Sunset, and its longest border is shared with Clearfield and Layton. Hill Field opened on November 7, 1940, and became Hill Air Force Base on February 5, 1948. Wartime employment peaked at just over 22,000 people in 1943.

The 75th Air Base Wing hosts the Ogden Air Logistics Complex, the 388th and 419th Fighter Wings and more than 50 other units. The Hill Aerospace Museum on base opened in 1981. For a Clearfield seller, the base means a steady pool of local buyers and renters, along with the occasional sudden move when someone gets orders and has little time to prepare a house.

How did Holladay start, and why does its history matter to a seller?

Holladay began in 1847, when pioneers from the Mississippi Company, including John Holladay of Alabama, reached the Salt Lake Valley and found a spring-fed stream they called Spring Creek near what is now Kentucky Avenue. A few men wintered in dugouts there, and the settlement took Holladay's name.

The area later went by Big Cottonwood and then Holladay-Cottonwood. The city was incorporated on November 29, 1999 as Holladay-Cottonwood. The name was shortened to Holladay on December 14, 1999. Liquefaction is most likely in low central parts of a valley with shallow groundwater, so risk varies from one lot to the next. The survey also says the maps show only general patterns and that a site-specific study by a Utah-licensed engineer and geologist is needed for a particular lot.

Older masonry is the main concern. Unreinforced brick buildings from roughly the 1920s to the 1960s were not designed for sideways ground motion. Sellers of Holladay brick houses from that era should expect buyers to ask about bracing and chimney anchors.

What is the history of Farmington?

Hector C. Haight wintered cattle in Farmington's grassy lowlands in 1847 and 1848, and five other families soon joined him. In 1852 the territorial legislature created Davis County and made the settlement, then called North Cottonwood, its county seat, renaming it Farmington.

Residents built Utah's first courthouse in 1854 and 1855, a two-story adobe building, and partly walled the town with mud. The Utah Central Railroad arrived in 1870, and the city incorporated on December 15, 1892 with 1,180 residents. Simon Bamberger developed the Lagoon resort in 1896, and it grew into Utah's largest amusement park.

The 2020 census counted 24,531 people, up from 18,275 in 2010. In 1990 the population was close to 10,000, so the city has more than doubled in about three decades.

Farmington allows two kinds of accessory units and a third option that lets an owner split a detached unit onto its own lot. Only one ADU is allowed per single-family home.

Either the main home or the ADU must be owner-occupied. A subordinate dwelling must be owner-occupied for two years after ownership is separated from the main home. The county page gives the deadline as September 16 in one place and September 15, 2026 in another, so confirm the date with Tax Administration at 801-451-3331 before filing.

Only the market value can be appealed, not the tax rate, and only the owner or an agent with a notarized authorization may file. Accepted evidence includes:

November 30, the statewide due date. Taxes unpaid after that date become delinquent, with a reduced penalty if everything is paid by January 31.

Which schools and utilities serve Hurricane?

The Washington County School District serves Hurricane. Hurricane High School teaches grades 10 to 12 and also draws students from La Verkin, Toquerville and Springdale, and the city has two elementary schools, an intermediate school for grades 6 and 7, a middle school for grades 8 and 9, and the charter school Valley Academy.

Hurricane runs its own electric utility. The American Public Power Association named Hurricane City Power a top-performing public power provider for 2024, the eighth national reliability award the utility has received, and the utility reported delivering power 99.9846% of the time. Fire protection comes through the Hurricane Valley Fire District, which the city's short-term rental rules reference.

The city offices are at 147 N 870 W, and the general number is 435-635-2811. The business license office is inside the Planning and Zoning Department, and a home-based business can be approved under Title 10, Chapter 42 of the city code.

What are Hurricane's short-term rental rules?

Hurricane requires a business license for any short-term rental, caps licenses in single-family zones, and does not allow another licensed rental within 300 feet. The rules are in Section 3-10-11 of the city code.

RuleHurricane requirement
License cap, single-family zonesThree licenses per 1,000 residents
SpacingNo other licensed rental within 300 feet
ParkingOne off-street space per bedroom

FinesUp to $750 per violation, and each day counts

A license does not follow the house automatically. The buyer must apply for a new license within 45 days of purchase, or the license is forfeited, and the owner would have to reapply or join the waiting list. A seller who markets a house as a rental should tell the buyer this up front, because the license can be part of what an investor is paying for.

How do Washington County property tax dates work?

Washington County real property tax is due November 30 each year, even if no notice arrives. The Treasurer's office does not offer payment plans, though partial payments of $10 or more per parcel are accepted at any time.

  • Payments apply first to interest, then penalty, then tax, and with several delinquent years Utah law sends money to the most recent year first.
  • Each May, the Clerk-Auditor sells properties that have been delinquent for at least five years.
  • Utah does not allow the sale of tax liens or tax lien certificates.
  • If neighbors received a notice and you did not, call the Treasurer for a copy.

Taxes are a lien against the property, not the owner, and the title company prorates them when a house sells mid-year. The Treasurer is at 111 East Tabernacle St. in St. George, phone 435-301-7720.

Valuation appeals follow state law: the later of September 15 or 45 days after the auditor gives notice. A home that is a primary residence is taxed on 55% of market value, and a buyer must file a new claim for the exemption after a sale.

What happens at closing for a Hurricane sale?

A Hurricane sale closes at a title company, and the deed is recorded with the Washington County Recorder at 111 East Tabernacle in St. George. The Recorder does not accept recordings after 4:45 p.m. Mountain Time, and its phone number is 435-301-7680.

State law requires a deed to name the grantees, give a mailing address for tax billing and carry a proper legal description. The signer's name needs to match the owner of record, which is worth checking early on an inherited house.

What do Hurricane sellers typically weigh?

Hurricane sellers choose between listing with an agent, selling on their own, or taking a cash offer. A listing means preparing the house for showings in a market with new construction nearby, while a cash sale lets the house sell as it is.

  • Empty houses that still carry tax, utility and insurance costs.
  • Short-term rentals that lost a license or fell short of the city rules.
  • Inherited houses with out-of-state heirs.
  • Older homes with aging roofs, evaporative coolers or failing air conditioning.

Ask any buyer for the closing date and proof of funds in writing, and compare the result against a listing's net after repairs and commission.

November 30 each year, billed by the Washington County Treasurer, even if you did not get a notice. The office offers no payment plans, though partial payments of $10 or more are accepted.

No. The buyer must apply for a new license within 45 days of the purchase or the license is forfeited. The buyer could then face a waiting list.

Is Hurricane's climate hard on houses?

It can be. Nearby St. George averages a July high near 102 degrees and about 60 days a year at 100 or above, so roofs, cooling systems and exterior finishes take heavy wear.

Where is a deed recorded for a Hurricane house?

At the Washington County Recorder's office in St. George. It does not accept recordings after 4:45 p.m. Mountain Time, and the title company usually handles the filing.
